intro: Scarbo is the creature who scratches at the bed curtains, vanishes and comes back larger than the room. Ravel gives him whispered repeated notes, enormous leaps and silences long enough to make the next sound a shock.

sections.label: A · Low notes and whispered drumming
sections.mNote: A trembling note answers the low opening figure

sections.label: B · Leaps across the keyboard
sections.mNote: Vif: the two hands spring apart

sections.label: Dev · Repeated notes and rising chords
sections.mNote: Short figures return in larger leaps and chords

sections.label: A′ · The low whisper returns
sections.mNote: The opening drumming descends into the bass

sections.label: B′ · The dance starts again
sections.mNote: Quick figures emerge from the low repeated notes

sections.label: Dev · The last assault of chords
sections.mNote: Leaps and repeated chords fill the keyboard

sections.label: Coda · The dwarf disappears
sections.mNote: Quiet repeated chords flicker out without slowing

cues.title: Something beneath the bed
cues.text: Three low notes rise out of the piano. A quiet repeated note trembles underneath a held chord, then stops. Ravel puts a fermata over the silence and marks it très long — very long.
cues.evidence: Durand score (1909), plate D. & F. 7207, p. 23: opening low figure, très fondu, en trémolo, and très long fermata. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/6a/IMSLP246875-PMLP02576-Ravel,_Maurice-Gaspard_de_la_nuit_Durand_7207_scan.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The dwarf springs up
cues.text: The piano accelerates through rising figures and arrives at Vif. The hands leap apart, pulling bass notes and high chords into the same quick dance. Sudden rests still cut holes in it.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 23–24: En accélérant, Vif, widely separated hands and rests after the first outburst.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A nail on silk
cues.text: Bertrand’s narrator hears Scarbo laughing in his alcove, then “grincer son ongle sur la soie des courtines de mon lit” — “his nail scraping the silk curtains of my bed”. The dwarf spins on one foot and rolls around the room like a witch’s dropped spindle.
cues.evidence: Aloysius Bertrand, Scarbo, Gaspard de la nuit, Mercure de France edition (1895), pp. 247–248, second and third paragraphs; our translation. https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(%C3%A9d._1895)/Scarbo_2

cues.title: Three notes, enormous hands
cues.text: The opening’s little rising figure keeps returning in new octaves. Repeated notes and leaps do much of the work: the pianist must turn tiny shapes into great bursts of chords without losing their sharp edges.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 23–42: recurring rising three-note figure, repeated-note writing and octave displacement.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: The whisper comes back
cues.text: The opening returns with its low three-note figure, held chord and repeated-note tremble. This time the drumming sinks further into the bass. Ravel asks for the soft pedal and leaves the upper piano almost empty.
cues.evidence: Durand score, pp. 34–35: reprise of the opening, sourdine, low repeated notes and subsequent ppp bass writing.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: As high as a cathedral
cues.text: The dwarf grows between the narrator and the moon “comme le clocher d’une cathédrale gothique” — “like the tower of a Gothic cathedral”. A little golden bell shakes on his pointed cap. Bertrand lets something absurd become immense.
cues.evidence: Bertrand, Scarbo, Mercure de France edition (1895), p. 248, fourth paragraph; our translation. https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(%C3%A9d._1895)/Scarbo_2

cues.title: A candle goes out
cues.text: The piano retreats into tiny repeated chords and a final dart up the keys. Ravel writes Sans ralentir, without slowing. Bertrand’s last words are “et soudain il s’éteignait” — “and suddenly he went out”, like a candle.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 42: ppp repeated chords and Sans ralentir. Bertrand, Scarbo, final sentence, Mercure de France edition (1895), p. 248; our translation. https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(%C3%A9d._1895)/Scarbo_2
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The silence breaks into leaps
transitions.from: A · Low notes and whispered drumming
transitions.how: After the held silences, rising piano figures accelerate. At Vif, the hands spring apart: low notes answer high chords, and a crescendo runs from pp to ff. Two bars of rests interrupt the burst before the moving accompaniment starts again.
transitions.evidence: Durand score (1909), pp. 23–24: En accélérant, Vif, crescendo and rests.

transitions.title: The low three notes return
transitions.from: Dev · Repeated notes and rising chords
transitions.how: The running figures fall away and the opening’s three low notes return under the soft pedal. The held chord and repeated-note tremble follow them, with another fermata. Ravel then moves the drumming down into the bass at ppp.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, pp. 34–35: return of the introduction and its descent into the bass.

transitions.title: The chords become a flicker
transitions.from: Dev · The last assault of chords
transitions.how: The wide arpeggios contract into quiet repeated chords above a low held bass. The pianist moves through short rests and little answering figures, then darts upwards to the last note. Sans ralentir keeps the ending quick.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, p. 42: ppp repeated chords, low pedal, final short figures and Sans ralentir.

composer.epithet: He made a ballet from two tunes and a snare drum, and gave his war dead a suite of dances.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery. His mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He kept returning to the Basque coast, and Spain kept returning in his music: the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera that rocks through the Rapsodie espagnole, the clocks ticking in a Toledo shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. Two teachers then understood him: André Gedalge, who gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and Fauré, whose composition class he entered in January 1898. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, became the pianist his music needed. Viñes gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces their composer could never have played with comparable command.
